title: Eighty years in robes
hookLine: the elder Bakkula, eighty years a monk and never ill

lines: AN OLD FRIEND, A LIFETIME LATER.
HOW LONG A MONK? EIGHTY YEARS.
cards: An old friend turns up after a lifetime apart, and the first thing out of his mouth is a question nobody else would dare ask. That's how the hundred and twenty-fourth discourse begins.
The elder Bakkula is staying near Rajagaha. A naked ascetic named Kassapa, a friend from Bakkula's lay days, comes to see him. How long have you been a monk, friend Bakkula?
Eighty years. Then Kassapa asks a blunt personal question about desire, and Bakkula doesn't answer it the way it's asked.

teach.b: You shouldn't ask it that way, Bakkula says.
Ask instead: in eighty years, how many times has a thought of sensual desire even come up? And he answers that one: not once. Then a long list follows, almost an inventory of a life.
In eighty years he never accepted a robe from a householder; he wore cast-off cloth. He never sat down to an invitation meal. He never leaned against a wall to rest, never lay down on a bed.

teach.h: NEVER ILL, NOT EVEN A MOMENT
teach.b: He never had an illness, not even for as long as it takes to pull a cow's teat, and never took so much as a piece of medicinal fruit. On the eighth day after he went forth, he says, he was freed.
Each item ends with the same refrain from the reciters: this too we remember as a wonderful quality of the venerable Bakkula.

teach.h: A KEY, AND A QUIET DEATH
teach.b: Kassapa is so moved he asks to go forth under him, and in time reaches the goal himself. Then the ending. One day Bakkula takes a key and goes from dwelling to dwelling: come out, venerables; today I'll pass away.

And he does, sitting among the monks. The Buddha never appears in this discourse. Bakkula's way was unusually strict, and plenty of Buddhists, then and now, take medicine, sit at invitations and wear donated robes.
What rings true across eighty years is simpler: a body used carefully, a life kept plain, and a death met sitting up, among friends.

how: In Theravada tradition Bakkula is remembered as the monk foremost in good health, and the rag-robe and solitary practices he kept are among the optional ascetic practices (dhutanga) some forest monks still take up today.

o: the naked ascetic who asked a blunt question
the physician who cared for the monks
an elder who was a monk for eighty years

games.q: eighty years in robes: tap the pairs.
p: the old friend who asked the blunt question
carried from dwelling to dwelling at the end

s: the Buddha teaches Bakkula in MN 124
the Buddha never appears in this discourse; it's about Bakkula and his old friend.
Bakkula refuses to answer the question as Kassapa asks it
he reframes it: ask how often a thought of desire even came up.
Kassapa leaves offended and never returns
he asks to go forth under Bakkula, and in time reaches the goal himself.

games.q: you're eighty years a monk, and you know today is your last day. what does Bakkula do?
o: he goes to bed and rests alone.
he goes from dwelling to dwelling with a key, inviting the monks to come out.
games.why: he tells the monks today he will pass away, and dies sitting in their midst.

practice: Bodies differ, and this isn't about comparing with Bakkula's health. Move your attention slowly through the body, and wherever something is working, a hand that holds, lungs that fill, eyes that read, give it a silent thank you.
Where something hurts, just acknowledge it carried you here too.

wordCard.voice: Bakkula. The elder who spent eighty years a monk, never ill even for a moment, and met his death sitting among the monks.

carryVoice: Your line: a life kept plain. Care for a body can be simple. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 1, Etadagga Vagga (Bakkula foremost in good health)
